Score the test stage for blocking

Source: R/fba-blocking.R
score_blocking.Rd

Records, for every test trial of every participant, whether the response is consistent with blocking and the confidence rating signed accordingly. The result is the per-trial table from which index_blocking() computes the blocking indices of each participant.

Usage

score_blocking(x, silence = FALSE)

Arguments

x

A catlas_rawdata object.

silence

Logical(1). Suppress the message summarising what was scored and how. Defaults to FALSE (recommended).

Value

A tibble with one row per participant/test trial combination, i.e., per participant, test block and test pair, and columns:

id

Participant identifier.

block

Test block.

cue1, cue2

The test pair, in canonical order.

blocked, control

The cue of the pair blocked in Stage 2 and its control cue.

expected

The outcome blocking predicts: the Stage 3 outcome associated with the control as opposed to the blocked cue.

timed_out

Whether the trial ended without a response.

response

The chosen outcome, NA when timed out.

consistent

response == expected, i.e., whether the response is consistent with blocking; NA when timed out.

confidence

The confidence rating; NA when timed out, and throughout in a design that collects no confidence ratings.

signed_confidence

confidence when consistent, -confidence otherwise; NA when either is missing.

Details

Consistency with blocking

Every test pair combines a cue blocked in Stage 2 with a control cue that was paired with the other outcome in Stage 3. If participants learned less about the blocked cues than about the control cues during Stage 3, they ought to choose the Stage 3 outcome of the control cue (Beesley & Le Pelley, 2011). The design registry records which outcome was paired with the control and which with the blocked cue for every test pair, and consistent is derived from it and the response.

The jsPsych column is_correct contains the same comparison as made by the experiment build. The function aborts if any answered test trial disagrees with the registry, or if a test trial presents a pair the design does not list. An experiment build whose expectations differed from the registry would otherwise flip the sign of the indices on the pairs concerned. Data bundles built with the current version of build_fba_rawdata() are checked when they are built as well.

Blocking test

The function scores a compound negation test (Don & Livesey, 2018), known in older literature as a conflict test (Gluck & Bower, 1988). In it, every test trial presents two cues that were paired with different outcomes during training, here a cue blocked in Stage 2 and a control cue paired with the other outcome in Stage 3, and asks which outcome follows the compound. The answer is a discrete choice among the outcomes of the test, i.e., an N-alternative forced choice (N-AFC, with N the number of outcomes), optionally followed by a confidence rating.

Currently, only the three-stage forward blocking designs with a context change between Stages 2 and 3 record such test pairs in the design registry. For any other design, the function aborts. Single-cue tests, in which the association of each cue with an outcome is rated or chosen separately, are not scored. Other designs and tests will be added once the need arises, e.g., when the CATLAS project runs a different kind of experiment.

Confidence ratings

The design registry records the scale of the confidence ratings (1 to 10 in the three-stage designs, as in Beesley & Le Pelley, 2011). In a design that collects no confidence ratings, confidence and signed_confidence are NA throughout, so that the table keeps the same columns in every design, and the confidence-weighted index of index_blocking() is NA too.

Messages

Every call states what was scored, how the sign is defined, the confidence scale, and how many trials timed out, unless silenced (silence = TRUE).

References

Beesley, T., & Le Pelley, M. E. (2011). The influence of blocking on overt attention and associability in human learning. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Animal Behavior Processes, 37(1), 114-120. doi:10.1037/a0019526

Don, H. J., & Livesey, E. J. (2018). Is the blocking effect sensitive to causal model? It depends how you ask. In Proceedings of the 40th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society (pp. 1633-1638).

Gluck, M. A., & Bower, G. H. (1988). From conditioning to category learning: An adaptive network model. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 117(3), 227-247. doi:10.1037/0096-3445.117.3.227
